narration: Your 401k match is costing you $94,000. I know — everyone says grab the match, it's free money. They're half right. The match is free. The account you're putting it in is the problem. Here's the math. If you make $80,000 and contribute 6% to a traditional 401k for 35 years at 8%, you retire with about $1.4 million. But every dollar comes out taxed as ordinary income. At a realistic 22% effective rate in retirement, you lose roughly $308,000 to the IRS. Now run the same numbers in a Roth 401k — same match, same growth, zero tax on the back end. The difference, after taxes, is about $94,000 in your pocket. Most people default into traditional because HR set it that way in 2009 and nobody updated it. Twenty seconds in your benefits portal flips the switch. The match still hits. The growth still compounds. The IRS just doesn't get a cut at the worst possible time — when you actually need the money. So which one are you in right now — traditional or Roth? Drop it in the comments. narration: Lifestyle inflation will cost you $1.2 million. Not your rent. Not your car. The slow creep nobody flags. Here's how it works. You get a raise — say $8,000 a year. Your old life cost what it cost. The honest move is to bank the raise, or at least half. The actual move? Nicer apartment. Better groceries. The upgraded phone plan. Within ninety days, the entire raise is absorbed. Now do that every two years for thirty years. If you'd invested just half of each raise at 8%, you'd have roughly $1.2 million extra at retirement. The cruel part — your standard of living barely changed each time. You can't even remember what you upgraded to. That's the trap. Lifestyle inflation doesn't feel like spending. It feels like normal. Rich people have a rule for this: every raise gets split before it hits checking. Fifty percent to investing, fifty percent to life. Automated. Boring. Brutal at scale. narration: The Augusta Rule lets you pocket up to $14,000 a year completely tax-free. And almost nobody uses it. Here's the actual law. Section 280A of the tax code says if you rent out your personal home for 14 days or fewer in a year, that rental income is 100% tax-free. Zero. It was originally written so Augusta, Georgia homeowners could rent to Masters tournament attendees without paying tax. But here's the move. If you own a business — even a side hustle LLC — your business can rent your home for legitimate meetings, strategy days, board sessions. Up to 14 days a year. At fair market rate. Your business deducts the expense. You receive the income tax-free. If comparable venues in your city run $1,000 a day, that's $14,000 of pure, legal, tax-free income. Annually. Forever. You need three things: a real business purpose, documented meetings, and a defensible market rate. That's it. The IRS knows about it. It's legal. It's just obscure enough that 97% of small business owners never claim it. So — did you know this existed? Comments. Subscribe for more legal loopholes the wealthy use weekly.
